item.title: Reinforcement learning to design near-perfect acoustic absorbers
item.description: arXiv:2611.15422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is proposed as a strategy for the multi-objective design of Helmholtz resonators with near-perfect acoustic absorption. The approach formulates resonator design as a sequential decision-making problem in which geometrical parameters are iteratively updated to balance competing objectives, including resonator volume, resonance frequency, and acoustic reflection. A Q-learning algorithm based on a neural network is developed to explore the design space and identify non-dominated solutions, providing a Pareto front of optimal configurations. The acoustic response is evaluated using a transfer matrix method that incorporates viscothermal losses and acoustic end corrections. Three representative designs are subsequently investigated using full-wave finite element simulations, showing good agreement in their absorption and reflection spectra and validating the accuracy of the reduced-order model. Finally, one optimized resonator is fabricated by three-dimensional printing and experimentally characterized in an impedance tube. The measured absorption coefficient reaches approximately 95\% near the resonance frequency, in agreement with the numerical predictions. These results demonstrate the potential of reinforcement learning for the automated design of compact acoustic absorbers and establish a computationally efficient framework combining multi-objective optimization, numerical modelling, and experimental validation.
item.dc:creator: M. Novelli, R. Arnau, L. M. Garcia-Raffi, V. Romero-Garc\'ia

item.title: Sparse, admissible and interpretable: discovery of isotropic limit surfaces with extended invariant libraries, physically gated mixtures of experts, and end-to-end structural identification
item.description: arXiv:2611.15476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Choosing and fitting a limit surface, a yield or failure criterion, to multiaxial strength tests is a model-selection problem with physical side conditions. The equivalent stress concept provides a catalogue of criteria with admissibility conditions: convexity, a unique surface definition, explicit solvability, and bounds on inelastic Poisson ratios. We recast the task as sparse, constrained, differentiable model discovery and compare three representations. The first is a library of invariant monomials I1^a q^m r3^c containing classical criteria as sparse members. The second extends this library by trigonometric Lode-angle terms, restricted by isotropy to cosine modes, and Podgorski-Bigoni-Piccolroaz (PBP) atoms with learnable shape parameters. The third is a mixture of convex gauge experts using either a competition (smooth-maximum) or direction gate with hard-concrete and Gumbel-softmax sparsity. A ray-wise first-root definition gives explicit solvability and an exactly differentiable objective. Convexity and absence of re-entrant branches are differentiable penalties for the libraries and hold by construction for the competition gate. That gate acts as a physically motivated regime selector between mechanisms. Under stated assumptions its responsibilities are the share of failure probability in Weibull statistics, the share of dissipation in Koiter's multi-surface flow rule, and a Boltzmann weight in Gibbs principles. In synthetic benchmarks, the extended library recovers truths like Mohr-Coulomb and PBP surfaces within 1% error. We analyse five experimental datasets: two PMI foams, PA6, concrete, and TSSA in Hencky-strain space. A sharp Lode function matters more than many terms. With PBP atoms, concrete data are fitted with a fourfold lower error. End-to-end identification from notched-bar loads via differentiable finite elements removes nominal-stress mapping bias.
item.dc:creator: Michael A. Kraus

item.title: Establishing Standards for Assessment and Reporting of SNSPD Performance
item.description: arXiv:2611.14653v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) can be made sensitive to single photons with near-unity detection efficiency, ultra-low dark-count rates, and sub-nanosecond timing jitter over a broad wavelength range. However, many studies report data inconsistently, often emphasizing a single performance metric without considering overall device performance. This inconsistent data reporting limits the field, as it makes it difficult to determine which device characteristics are most important. Different applications require functionalities that may conflict with one another; for example, longer-wavelength operation may require lower operating temperatures. Moreover, there is no universally accepted metric for defining the figures of merit of an SNSPD. In this work, we amass a dataset representing the state of the art of SNSPD fabrication, including operating temperature, operating wavelength, photon count rates (PCR), and dark count rates (DCR). We fit the PCR curves and suggest using the saturation plateau length to gauge the SNSPD's sensitivity. We then fit the DCR and compare the PCR and DCR. Using this approach, we establish a quantitative framework to determine the optimal biasing condition for a given device and to determine the device's sensitivity at that optimal biasing condition, enabling meaningful comparisons across disparate devices. Additionally, we offer concrete benchmarks for measuring device performance.
item.dc:creator: Ari N. Willner, Alejandro Simon, Reed A. Foster, Francesca Incalza, Ava A. Brule, Philip Donald Keathley, Karl K. Berggren

item.title: SunLightBots: Turning sunlight into self-sustained, high-power motion in soft robots
item.description: arXiv:2611.14729v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Soft robots built from active materials can directly convert environmental stimuli into motion, offering a route to energy autonomy and embodied control. However, environmental energy is generally harvested at low power, whereas rapid, mechanically demanding actions require high mechanical output power. Reconciling this mismatch while sustaining self-regulated cyclic actuation is challenging, particularly at the subgram scale, where limited payload capacity constrains the integration of conventional power and control hardware. Here, we present SunLightBots, a class of subgram, sunlight-powered, untethered soft robots that achieve autonomous locomotion under continuous illumination near 1 Sun (100 mW/cm2). Their operation is enabled by a self-resetting snapping (SRS) mechanism that integrates liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) with snap-through instability to accumulate solar energy supplied at low power, release it as rapid, high-power motion, and reset through photothermal-mechanical feedback. Through coordinated optimization of the LCE actuation temperature, photothermal conversion, actuation stress, and structural energy barrier, the system operates near 1 Sun and achieves a peak mass-specific mechanical power of 89 W/kg. At this irradiance, the optimized LCE generates an actuation stress of 0.1 MPa at approximately 60 deg C. SunLightBots demonstrate sustained swimming, crawling, and repeated impulsive jumping. Under 1.5 Suns, the swimmer advances more than three body lengths per cycle. This work provides a materials-mechanics route toward autonomous soft robots powered entirely by the environment.
item.dc:creator: Yoo Jin Lee, Melanie Torres Crespo, Zhongxiao Deng, Andrew Tejada-Vega, Rebecca Kramer-Bottiglio, Wenzhong Yan, Yimin Luo

item.title: Beyond Ground States: Learning Many-Body Hamiltonians for p-Bit Invertible Arithmetic
item.description: arXiv:2611.14744v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Probabilistic-bit (p-bit) invertible logic encodes a Boolean relation as an energy whose ground states are its legal assignments, computing in any direction by sampling. Traditional constructions target ground-state membership and a wide minimum energy gap, yet finite-time samplers traverse excited states. We cast Hamiltonian design as inverse statistical mechanics: fit an energy with interactions up to order four whose Gibbs law approaches uniformity on each clamp case's legal states, under a gap floor keeping every legal state below every illegal one. Constrained maximum likelihood with pruning and refitting fits terms from a fixed pool, and every delivered energy is audited exactly on all cases. Each energy is scored by time to a verified solution under restarts with its best of nine tuned samplers. In underdetermined modes, learned multipliers factor in 0.55, 0.44, 0.52 and 0.46 [0.38, 0.56] of the hand-written encodings' updates from 4x4 to 7x7, faster within every family below 7x7 at no resolved work penalty; learned adders solve the reverse mode in 0.71 of the updates at 8 bits and about a quarter at 24 and 32 bits, at 0.55 of the work at 32 bits. At 5x5 under equal pool, budget and floor, a gap-maximizing fit reaches 0.79 [0.73, 0.88] in updates and 1.26 in work against the hand-written encoding, while likelihood fitting takes 0.55 [0.46, 0.58] and 0.58 [0.48, 0.61] of the gap fit's updates and work. Rounding coefficients to the narrowest exact integer words tested, we run both energies at each pair's common word on one FPGA color-sweep SSA core, bit-exact with software: learned multipliers take 0.41 of the hand-written encoding's cycles at 4x4 and 0.057 [0.045, 0.068] at 7x7, at up to 2.4 times its lookup tables. The method requires only a circuit's legal assignments; in determined modes, hand-written encodings take less work, and from 12 bits on the adder fewer updates.
item.dc:creator: Tian Feng, Xutang Fan, Yiyun Chen

item.title: Mach2: Scientific Discovery Platform with Deterministic Execution Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.14777v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language-model agents can formulate workflows and invoke specialized tools, yet compliance with natural-language operating rules is not guaranteed by prompting alone. Mach2 addresses this limitation by coupling Eigen orchestration to deterministic, lint-like checks of tool requests, source changes, acceptance tests, and artifact contracts. Domain requirements are represented as executable predicates: mandatory failures prevent advancement of the checked operation, while diagnostic findings are retained for correction or review. User-specified test-driven development (TDD), CodeGrapher's abstract-syntax-tree analysis, and history-guided evolutionary search provide complementary verification and optimization mechanisms. Mach2 also generates task-specific agent packages for execution through independently selected endpoints. The originating harness validates returned artifacts against declared interfaces and evidence requirements without assuming continuous supervision of the remote run. Model-internal-knowledge (MIK) dependencies are recorded separately from source-grounded and test-supported findings. This paper formalizes the rule-gated execution model and the agent-package lifecycle, and proposes measurable criteria for evaluating rule compliance, engineering validity, and cross-endpoint task continuity.
item.dc:creator: Vansh Sharma, Venkat Raman

item.title: High-directivity pulsed beams for effective power and information transfer
item.description: arXiv:2611.14860v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A vector spherical wave expansion (VSWE) is used to engineer an elemental multipole source whose radiated field is a superdirective, extremely unidirectional (SDEU) needle beam. It is proved analytically and confirmed numerically that the element attains Harrington's normal-directivity value along its beam axis. Its radiated field is linearly polarized with an azimuthally symmetric magnitude; its back lobe vanishes identically in the far field. The unidirectional behavior is quantified at any finite far-field radius by a closed-form front-to-back ratio, obtained from an exact per-degree cancellation of the electric and magnetic multipole contributions in the backward direction. Uniform circular arrays (UCAs) of these elements inherit the SDEU behavior. Driving the arrays with zero-area pulses (ZAPs) transfers the frequency-domain performance intact into the time domain. It is shown that whether the radiated energy beam is narrower or wider than the corresponding intensity beam is decided by a single property of the radiated waveform, not by the size of the radiating aperture. A simple single-cycle ZAP is used to quantify the performance of the UCAs; its energy beam is the narrower one. The same criterion is shown to govern the focal spot of near-field-focused pulse-driven arrays. A custom-designed intensity-enhancement (IE) ZAP is introduced that raises the focal intensity by almost 200-fold over a narrow-band reference while producing a focal spot more than ten times smaller in both the axial and transverse directions, deeply subwavelength with respect to its own effective wavelength. It is demonstrated that these stunning IE results are produced simply with an array of pulse-excited Huygens dipole sources. These results identify the pulse shape, rather than the aperture, as the design variable that governs localized electromagnetic energy and information delivery.
item.dc:creator: Richard W. Ziolkowski

item.title: Directed Domain Wall Motion by Radio-Frequency Currents
item.description: arXiv:2611.15305v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Magnetic domain walls (DWs) are central to emerging spintronic technologies for memory, logic and neuromorphic computing, where their controlled displacement is a key functionality. While current-induced DW motion driven by spin-orbit torques is well established under direct currents, it remains unclear how radio-frequency (RF) currents couple to DWs and whether they can generate directed motion under a symmetric periodic drive. Here we show that RF currents drive DW oscillations, which can be rectified into directed motion through symmetry breaking. Using time-resolved and static magneto-optical Kerr microscopy, we demonstrate that RF spin-orbit torques efficiently excite low-frequency DW oscillations well below the ferromagnetic resonance frequency. Whereas these oscillations remain symmetric in the absence of perturbations, symmetry breaking by a transverse magnetic field produces self-propulsion, while symmetry breaking by an initial current pulse gives rise to sustained DW motion. We further show that in initially uniform magnetic states, RF-driven expansion of a pulse-generated edge domain ultimately results in efficient RF-assisted magnetic switching. Together, these results establish a general framework for understanding how RF-driven DW oscillations are rectified into directed motion, providing new opportunities for their high-frequency control.
item.dc:creator: Lukas Fischer, Rouven Dreyer, Simon Arnold, Jae-Chun Jeon, Georg Woltersdorf, Stuart S. P. Parkin

item.title: A Magnetic Neuroevolution Potential for Large Scale Spin-Lattice Simulations
item.description: arXiv:2611.15395v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurately describing magnetic order, lattice vibrations, and their coupling at finite temperatures within a unified framework remains a major challenge in atomistic simulations of magnetic materials. In this work, we develop a magnetic neuroevolution potential that explicitly incorporates magnetic degrees of freedom, establishing a potential-energy description jointly determined by atomic structures and magnetic configurations and enabling unified predictions of atomic forces and magnetic energy gradients. Using CrN, Fe, and FeGe with collinear or noncollinear magnetic configurations as representative systems, we demonstrate that the model outperforms standard neuroevolution potentials without magnetic descriptors in predicting energies, atomic forces, and virials, while yielding equilibrium lattice constants consistent with experimental values. Phonon calculations for different magnetic states show that the model captures lattice vibrational responses to changes in magnetic order. Finite-temperature spin-lattice dynamics simulations further reveal the temperature dependence of magnetic excitation spectra, while calculations of the average atomic magnetic moment versus temperature demonstrate the influence of spin-lattice coupling on magnetic transition temperatures and system-size convergence. For Fe, explicitly including spin-lattice coupling brings the predicted magnetic transition temperature closer to experiment, whereas the difference in FeGe is smaller. Performance benchmarks demonstrate that the method enables coupled dynamics simulations of over two million atoms on a single consumer-grade GPU. By combining magnetic-configuration resolution with high computational efficiency, the framework provides an efficient tool for investigating finite-temperature dynamics and spin-lattice coupling in large-scale magnetic systems.
item.dc:creator: Rongkun Chen, Junhan Li, Feng Xiao, Shiqian Hu

item.title: Subwavelength registration of skull-compensating acoustic holograms via nonlinear parametric array feedback
item.description: arXiv:2611.15730v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Realizing the potential of optimized acoustic holograms for applications like transcranial ultrasound requires sub-wavelength alignment accuracy (less than 1.5 mm at 1 MHz), which is difficult to achieve with current non-MRI optical neuro-navigation methods. To address the critical challenge of alignment, we leverage the parametric array (PA) signal as an alignment surrogate, a highly penetrative, low-frequency difference wave generated by the nonlinear mixing of two primary high-frequency beams. Simulations show that a misaligned skull-compensating lens increases the primary acoustic energy within the skull bone (volumetric energy trapping), which strengthens the nonlinear source of the PA signal. We also tested whether shear-mode conversion in bone contributes: 2D elastic simulations showed only a small (3-5%) increase in shear-type motion with misalignment, and the transmitted ex vivo bursts did not lengthen as a shear path would require. Pseudo-sound and microbubble artifacts were examined and found unlikely to explain the signal, consistent with the PA signal arising from the intrinsic nonlinearity of the bone. Minimizing this PA signal yields a noninvasive real-time feedback mechanism that achieves sub-wavelength alignment accuracy, outperforming standard neuronavigation. Our findings present a robust framework that supports the design of simple, economical, and high-performance transcranial ultrasound systems for high-precision neuro-interventions.
item.dc:creator: Pradosh Pritam Dash, Costas D. Arvanitis

item.title: Metasurfaces with Anisotropic Electric and Magnetic Conductivities: Parameter Retrieval for Arbitrary Incidence and Polarization
item.description: arXiv:2611.15752v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Metasurfaces come in a great variety of unit cell geometries and material composition. A common approach for describing them relies on retrieving effective surface parameters (e.g., electric and magnetic conductivities) from plane-wave scattering data. Conventional retrieval methods are often limited to isotropic unit cells, a uniform host material, or lead to increased complexity by requiring reflection and transmission coefficients from both sides of the metasurface. Here, we derive analytical expressions for the equivalent surface conductivities of an electrically- and magnetically-polarizable anisotropic metasurface under oblique plane-wave incidence with arbitrary polarization. The proposed formulation does not require bidirectional scattering information, thus simplifying the process especially in experimental studies. The method is validated through representative electric and magnetic meta-atoms at microwave and THz frequencies, respectively. Their ability for polarization conversion is demonstrated and discussed relying on the physical insight provided by the retrieved anisotropic conductivities. In addition, we present the inverse expressions for calculating the reflection and transmission coefficients from known surface conductivity tensors, which can prove useful for metasurface synthesis and radiation problems.
item.dc:creator: Dimitrios Chatzidimitriou, Alexandros Pitilakis, Odysseas Tsilipakos

item.title: Integrated optical isolators enabled by 2D semiconductors via spin-momentum locking
item.description: arXiv:2611.16125v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Integrated optical isolators based on spin-momentum locking hold great potential for protecting photonic integrated circuits from unwanted reflections. Currently, the most common implementations are magneto-optical isolators that require an externally applied magnetic field. Nevertheless, a wide range of nonreciprocal effects remains to be exploited in alternative material platforms. Although the majority of these effects induce changes to the propagation of light as a function of its polarization, they can be directly connected to the propagation direction through spin-momentum locking. We employ a computational approach to investigate various designs of integrated isolators based on nonreciprocal 2D semiconductors, studying the influence of their geometry and optical properties on the device performance. Additionally, we propose a novel concept for an all-optical isolator based on spin-valley polarization and optically tunable magnetism in transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers. Our results establish 2D semiconductors as an advanced platform for integrated nonreciprocal devices, enabling functionalities that are difficult to achieve with conventional magneto-optical materials like all-optical operation.
item.dc:creator: Fernando Mart\'in-Romero, V\'ictor J. G\'omez, Alberto G. Curto

item.title: Bright and Uniform Silicon Carbide Nanophotonic Arrays for Scalable Nanoscale Quantum Sensing
item.description: arXiv:2611.16252v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Silicon carbide (SiC) spin defects are emerging as powerful platforms for nanoscale quantum sensing due to their near-surface stability, near-infrared emission, and CMOS compatibility. However, poor photon collection efficiency and the reliance on randomly distributed defects hinder the realization of practical, large-scale devices. Here, we demonstrate scalable, ultra-bright, and highly uniform SiC quantum nanophotonic arrays. By combining a self-aligned fabrication process with localized oxygen ion implantation, we deterministically position PL5 and PL6 centers at the exact center of 4H-SiC nanopillars. This architecture yields record-high photon count rates of $\sim$1 Mcps (PL5) and $\sim$2 Mcps (PL6), establishing a new benchmark for SiC color centers while maintaining near-identical brightness across the array. Furthermore, we apply these devices to nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), successfully demonstrating external nanoscale nuclear-spin detection. These results establish our SiC nanopillars as robust building blocks for scanning quantum probes and scalable sensor networks.
item.dc:creator: Chenyang Liao, Chihang Luo, Xin Chen, Cunliang Xin, Hongfang Zuo, Haoyu Sun, Fazhan Shi, Mengqi Wang, Ya Wang

item.title: Bare and stretched string tyre models with distributed FrBD dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2603.02869v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a novel class of string tyre models with FrBD friction dynamics. By modelling the distributed carcass and tread deformations with string-like equations, the resulting formulation leads to a system of semilinear parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs) that describe the evolution of the tyre states without explicitly distinguishing between stick and slip regimes. Rigorous stability and passivity analyses are also conducted using a Lyapunov-based approach, establishing boundedness of the distributed states and energy dissipation during rolling contact. The proposed Lyapunov function admits a clear physical interpretation as the total elastic energy stored in the tyre, enabling a direct link between mechanical energy storage and frictional dissipation due to slip losses. The steady-state and transient behaviours of the model are investigated both numerically and experimentally, revealing that the new formulation can satisfactorily reproduce nonlinear relaxation phenomena excited by step slip inputs. The resulting model provides a physically interpretable, mathematically well-posed, and computationally efficient basis for advanced vehicle dynamics simulations and control-oriented applications.
item.dc:creator: Luigi Romano

item.title: How do sub-bandgap reflectors affect the performance of photovoltaic modules?
item.description: arXiv:2604.20757v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sub-bandgap reflectors (SBR) can reduce the temperature of photovoltaic (PV) modules by reflecting the near-infrared region of the solar spectrum with photon energies smaller than the electronic bandgap of the solar cell absorber material. We consider an ideal SBR, which reflects 100% of non-harvestable low-energy photons but does not alter the reflectivity of the PV module for usable high-energy photons, and estimate how reducing the module temperature with the SBR affects the annual and the cumulative energy yield of silicon PV modules for six locations in North America and Europe. An ideal SBR would increase the annual energy yield between 0.9% and 1.4% for open-rack mounted modules and between 1.5% and 2.3% for close-roof mounted PV modules. Whether a non-ideal SBR provides a benefit in actual deployments strongly depends on the location and the optical properties of the coating. Beyond effects on the instantaneous power conversion efficiency and hence the annual energy yield, reducing the temperature by an SBR might also reduce the degradation and increase the overall lifetime of the PV module. By describing degradation using a simple Arrhenius approach with typical activation energies between 0.4 eV and 0.8 eV, we find that an ideal SBR increases the cumulative energy yield over 30 years between 2.2% and 4.0% for an open-rack mounted PV module in Princeton, New Jersey, USA.
item.dc:creator: Klaus J\"ager, Jyotirmoy Mandal, Barry P. Rand, Forrest Meggers, Christiane Becker

item.title: The role of distributed friction dynamics on heave-induced motion of offshore drilling systems: modelling, analysis, and simulations
item.description: arXiv:2610.22189v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper investigates the influence of friction dynamics on heave-induced disturbance propagation using a coupled hydraulic-structural drilling model formulated as a semilinear interconnection of ordinary and hyperbolic partial differential equations (ODE-PDEs), and capturing spatially distributed memory effects in the drillstring-wellbore interaction. First, local and global existence and uniqueness results are established, and sufficient conditions for boundedness and input-to-state stability are deduced via a small-gain analysis. Subsequently, extensive numerical investigations are carried out, including harmonic excitation studies, nonlinear distortion analysis, spatial amplification investigations, mechanism-isolation experiments, parameter sensitivity analysis, and broadband simulations under realistic offshore sea-state excitation. The simulation results indicate that, whilst the hydraulic response is governed primarily by wave propagation phenomena, compressibility, and boundary reflections, the structural dynamics display substantially greater sensitivity to distributed friction effects. Furthermore, drillstring-wellbore friction is shown to have a relatively limited influence on well-posedness but a potentially significant impact on stability margins. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for coupled hydraulic-structural dynamics and distributed friction mechanisms when analysing, monitoring, and controlling offshore drilling systems.
item.dc:creator: Luigi Romano, Ole Morten Aamo

item.title: Mechanisms of Zener diode and ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction: A novel explanation in terms of impurity-photovoltaic-effect resulting from infrared self-emission at room-temperature
item.description: arXiv:2611.12431v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In textbooks, a quantum-mechanical tunneling mechanism based on electron-wavefunction is used to explain Zener diode as well as ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction. In this study, an attempt in particle description is made to explain these devices. Any object at room-temperature emits infrared (IR) photons. The process of heavy doping can cause many defects. The self-absorption of the IR emission could be achieved through sub-band-gap excitations due to defects, creating carriers. In a heavily doped p-n junction device, some of the IR-generated carriers diffuse into the junction which has a built-in field. The built-in field sweeps out the carriers, creating IR photocurrent. The reverse leakage current of the p-n junction is regarded as the IR photocurrent according to a precedent where impurity-photovoltaic-effect is used to explain circuit devices (arXiv:2510.18226). Heavy doping results in not only a great many IR-generated carriers but also an avalanche effect at low voltage, producing Zener breakdown. Additionally, the impurity-photovoltaic-effect can make a reasonable contribution to explaining the temperature dependence of Zener breakdown. If the doping is very heavy, the heavily doped p-n junction can be altered to create an ohmic contact, which can also be explained in terms of impurity-photovoltaic-effect. Not only quantum mechanics, but also this photovoltaic mechanism in particle description can explain the above devices. Considering the wave-particle duality, the combination of quantum-mechanical and photovoltaic mechanisms is suggested to explain these devices. Each mechanism plays a big or small role in the explanation.
item.dc:creator: Jianming Li

item.title: Ultrafast Optical Probing of Laser Processing
item.description: arXiv:2509.03220v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Laser treatment has emerged into a cornerstone of industrial manufacturing. This creates the demand to understand in detail the involved physical processes and their dynamics, to control the process, and to keep guard in-situ the laser manufacturing steps. Given the contactless interaction of light with matter, particularly optical methods appear most suitable for probing laser processing. This chapter reviews the current scientific and technological state of analyzing laser-based material processing by short and ultrashort optical pulses. For that, sequential passive interrogation of material properties (via reflection, absorption, scattering, diffraction, interference, or specific nonlinear responses) can be employed through so-called pump-probe techniques (where the time-resolution is not given by the detector response time but by the duration of an electromagnetic probe pulse that is interrogating the transient scenery at a controlled delay (typ. fs to \mu s) with respect to the arrival of the pump laser pulse). These approaches are capable to analyze on microscopic to macroscopic scales a plethora of different processes involved in laser processing, such as heating, melting, ablation, plasma- and shockwave-formation, optical breakdown in surrounding liquids and gases, shielding and accumulation effects, surface solidification and restructuring, etc. A special focus is set on the variety of ultrafast optical imaging schemes for visualizing the dynamics of laser processing at the surface and in the bulk of the irradiated materials, including photography and microscopy, holography, tomography, ptychography, and coherent diffractive imaging. The chapter provides a historic survey, highlights important scientific and technological developments and breakthroughs, discusses selected applications, explores the requirements and current limitations, and sheds light on emerging future trends.
item.dc:creator: J\"orn Bonse

item.title: How Does Incubation Affect Laser Material Processing?
item.description: arXiv:2509.08326v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the last decades, the subject of laser-induced damage (LID) moved from a topic of scientific interest toward laser material processing for technical applications. When using pulsed lasers, the cumulative effect known as incubation is one of the most fundamental features of the processing event. Incubation manifests by the fact that the critical fluence for LID (known as laser-induced damage threshold, LIDT) depends on the number of pulses N exciting one spot on the sample. In most cases, the threshold fluence decreases with N starting from the single-shot ablation threshold and remains constant for large N. No ablation or damage occurs for any N, if the fluence is kept below the multiple-pulse threshold. In contrast, examples where the LIDT increases with N have been reported. The latter effect is known as laser conditioning and is advantageously used when ramping up the power of high-power laser systems. Incubation has been described for many types of solids; the motivation for these comprehensive efforts is twofold. Firstly, one tries to prevent the damage of optical materials in the beam path of high-energy or high-peak-power lasers. Secondly, one deliberately uses this damage for the sculpting of components. In this chapter, we introduce the reader to the mechanisms of incubation. We are going to look at the parameters controlling LID and highlight the peculiarity of the parameter "number of pulses". We will give an overview of the experimental work done in a variety of materials. There are several physical and chemical mechanisms proposed that govern incubation, and there are several mathematical models to describe the behavior of threshold fluence and ablation rate in dependence on the number of pulses. In a few cases, the two classes of mechanisms are even related to each other. Eventually, we will show the implications that incubation has on real-world laser machining.
item.dc:creator: Matthias Lenzner, J\"orn Bonse

item.title: Magneto-optical signal from $\mathrm{Co_2Mn}$-based Heusler thin films in MOKE and BLS
item.description: arXiv:2608.07052v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: $\mathrm{Co_2Mn}$-based Heusler compounds offer a versatile, composition-tunable platform for magnonics and spintronics. Among them, the half-metallic $\mathrm{Co_2MnSi}$ is of particular interest for magnonics owing to its ultralow Gilbert damping, yet its weak magneto-optical response in the visible challenges optical probing such as Brillouin light scattering (BLS). We study the magneto-optical response of epitaxial $\mathrm{Co_2Mn}X$ films ($X = \{\mathrm{Al}_x\mathrm{Si}_{1-x}, \mathrm{Ga}_x\mathrm{Ge}_{1-x}, \mathrm{Sn}\}$) by magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) spectroscopy and BLS. Angle-resolved MOKE resolves a significant, wavelength-dependent quadratic MOKE (QMOKE) only for $\mathrm{Co_2MnSi}$, whereas $\mathrm{Co_2MnAl}$, $\mathrm{Co_2MnGa}$ and $\mathrm{Co_2MnSn}$ respond dominantly linearly. Comparing BLS intensities of thermal magnons at two wavelengths, $\mathrm{Co_2MnSi}$ gives the weakest signal at 532 nm yet among the strongest at 457 nm, tracking the spectral dependence of its Kerr angle. These results emphasise the relation between the two magneto-optical techniques, guiding the choice of probing wavelength for $\mathrm{Co_2Mn}$-based Heusler compounds, and provide a transferable approach for other magnetic materials.
item.dc:creator: Anna Maria Friedel, Nicolas Fermon, Tobias B\"ottcher, S\'ebastien Petit-Watelot, St\'ephane Andrieu, Philipp Pirro

item.title: Coupled Electronic Structure and Phonon Transport Driven by Bonding Reconstruction in Ba-B-C Clathrates
item.description: arXiv:2609.32894v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Composition-driven changes in electron count, structural symmetry and bonding environment can couple the electronic and thermal responses in a material. Here, with density-functional theory and machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), we compare cubic BaB3C3 with its B-C substituted tetragonal counterpart, BaB2C4. The additional valence electron and accompanying change in crystal symmetry drive a transition from metallic BaB3C3 to semiconducting BaB2C4 and the formation of short/strong C-C bonds. The reconstructed bonding network hardens the phonon spectrum, with the maximum frequency increasing from 800 to 900. At room temperature, the in-plane lattice thermal conductivity increases from 7.6 to 18.7 W/mK, while the thermal transport alters from isotropic to anisotropic for BaB2C4. This enhancement is associated with the strengthened bonding network, higher phonon frequencies/group velocities, longer lifetimes and larger mean free paths. Machine learning potentials accurately reproduced the DFT-level energies and forces with negligible errors, and the harmonic and anharmonic features are benchmarked against explicit first-principles calculations. Our findings demonstrate that minimal B-C substitution provides a viable strategy to link composition- and structure-associated bonding reconstruction with correlated electronic and phononic alterations.
item.dc:creator: Ghulam Hussain, Dario Massa, Muhammad Usman, Rajibul Islam, Magdalena Birowska, Carmine Autieri, Xiaoguang Li
